messages.subject: Re: Line length in complex topography
parts:
I was a little confused by the response to this question.

>>> > >> Intuitively, since inferences are 2 dimensional, A seems to me to be the
>> >> correct choice. However, if some parts of the study area are more complex
>> >> than others, the actual distance walked will be greater on some transects of
>> >> the same mapped length and more animals may be counted on those transects.
>> >> Does this pose any practical or theoretical problems?

> > You didn't ... perhaps this is something we should include in the next
> > edition. You're right - A is correct. We have to work with 2D
> > projections simply because the surface area is a function of the scale you
> > measure it at ... the finer the scale, the greater the surface area. This
> > is related to measuring the length of a coastline ... which gets
> > progressively longer as your data get more precise.
> > So densities on steep slopes have the potential to be greater simply
> > because there is more habitat available per flat km^2.

During survey work on chameleons in Malagasy rainforest, we use 50 m tape
measures as our transect lines (3 tapes per transect - searching on hands
and knees for several hours). These are set by hand and must therefore
follow the contours of the land (answer B). The densities that we have
calculated thus relate directly to the actual distance walked, not those
that have been projected onto a 2D map. Are 2D projections only relevant for
large surveys, ie those running for several km?

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Line length in complex topography
parts:
> > During survey work on chameleons in Malagasy rainforest, we use 50 m tape
> > measures as our transect lines (3 tapes per transect - searching on hands
> > and knees for several hours). These are set by hand and must therefore
> > follow the contours of the land (answer B). The densities that we have
> > calculated thus relate directly to the actual distance walked, not those
> > that have been projected onto a 2D map. Are 2D projections only relevant for
> > large surveys, ie those running for several km?

Densities are OK. The problem comes if you want to estimate abundance -
you have to define an area to multiply your density estimate by - and that
really only makes sense for a 2D projection of area. In surveys for deer
that we designed, we had this problem, and tried correcting our abundance
estimates to take account of the fact that measured lengths of transects
differed from the corresponding horizontal projections. Although the
ground was very hilly, the corrections proved to be sufficiently small
that we could ignore them.

Contour transects avoid the issue, though create other issues. For
example, if the transects are curved, density estimates are
biased. Degree of bias depends on degree of curvature. Also, it is
difficult to get approximately uniform probability of cover when using
contour transects, which could generate bias if density is a function of
altitude. Variances estimated from replicate lines also tend to be large
when contour transects are used, because line-to-line variation tends to
be larger if density is a function of altitude.

Steve Buckland
